name: heaven

attributes.attribute: not opposed to nor paired with earth in Celtic cosmology
no myth of the marriage or forced separation of heaven and earth
Celtic world-view like that of shamanic cultures
the Celts placed the dead and divine in the Otherworld, never in the sky

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Heaven is a cosmological concept in Celtic thought. The Celts did not generally imagine heaven and earth as opposed to each other, nor did they pair them as complements. No myth of a marriage of heaven and earth survives, nor of their forced separation, such as other cultures tell. Fragmentary myths suggest a worldview like that of shamanic cultures. In Judeo-Christian cosmology heaven is the abode of the dead and the divine. The Celts placed both in the Otherworld instead. They found that Otherworld out at sea, under a hill, or in an invisible universe parallel to ours. It was never in the sky.

okr.objective: Document heaven as the Celtic cosmological concept unlike the sky abode.
key_results: Record that the Celts did not oppose heaven and earth.
Note the Otherworld location of the dead and divine, never in the sky.
evidence: Monaghan, P. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore (2008): heaven entry.
